opus-5.5.text:
I think the two are much more tightly connected than people from the outside usually assume. There's a common picture where research teams sit in one corner pushing capability forward, and then a separate product team takes whatever comes out and wraps it into something users can touch. In practice it doesn't really work that way, at least not in the most productive periods.

The way I see it, product is actually one of the strongest sources of signal for research. When you put a model in front of millions of people, you immediately learn things you would never discover from benchmarks: where it fails, what people actually want it to do, which behaviors feel "intelligent" and which ones feel brittle. That feedback flows straight back into what the research agenda should prioritize. So product isn't just the downstream consumer of intelligence, it's part of the loop that defines what better intelligence even means.

At the same time, there's a real tension, and I don't want to pretend it's not there. Products want stability, predictability, and fast iteration on things users can see. Frontier research often needs room for bets that might not pay off for a long time, or might fail entirely. If everything gets pulled toward the next product milestone, you risk optimizing locally and missing the bigger jumps. So the organization constantly has to balance: how much effort goes into making today's model more useful, and how much goes into things that might only matter two or three generations from now.

My personal view is that the core driver is still intelligence. If the underlying model becomes fundamentally more capable, a lot of product problems simply disappear, or new products become possible that nobody would have designed in advance. But you only get there efficiently if you stay grounded in real usage. So I'd describe it as: intelligence is the engine, and product is both the steering wheel and the road test. You really need both, and the best progress happens when the people working on them talk to each other every day rather than handing things over the wall.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence and product development as tightly connected and mutually informing, not roughly orthogonal.

r002.rationale: It says greater model capability can make possible new products “nobody would have designed in advance,” conveying that products built around capabilities that do not yet exist are hard to envision.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two were always meant to be intertwined, though it wasn't obvious from the outside for a long time.

When I was at OpenAI, the mission was clearly about advancing intelligence. The research was the center of gravity. Products, in the early days, were almost an afterthought, or at least they were treated as a way to validate what the research could do rather than as a goal in themselves. But what I came to appreciate is that products are not just downstream of intelligence. They are one of the most important feedback loops for it.

Think about what happened with ChatGPT. Before it launched, the models existed. GPT-3.5 was there. But nobody inside fully understood what people actually wanted to do with it, where it failed, what felt magical and what felt broken. The moment you put it in front of millions of people, you get signal you could never generate in a lab. That signal shapes what you train next, what you measure, what capabilities you prioritize. So the product becomes a kind of instrument for discovering what intelligence should look like.

At the same time, there's a real tension. Research wants long horizons and tolerates failure. Products want reliability and iteration on weekly cycles. If you let the product side dominate, you end up optimizing for the next quarter and you stop making the big bets that actually move the frontier. If you let research dominate completely, you build beautiful things that don't touch the world. OpenAI's culture, at least during my time, was constantly negotiating that balance, and it wasn't always comfortable.

My own view, and this shaped how I think about my work now, is that the most interesting progress happens when you treat them as one system. You advance intelligence so that new products become possible, and you build products so that intelligence has a place to learn what matters. Reinforcement learning is a nice metaphor here. The environment matters as much as the agent. Deploying a model into the real world is, in a sense, giving the intelligence a much richer environment than any benchmark.

So I don't see it as research versus product. I see product as the environment where intelligence gets tested and, ultimately, where it earns the right to keep improving.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence and products as intertwined and ultimately “one system,” rather than roughly orthogonal pursuits.

r002.rationale: It says people did not fully understand how users would use existing models, but does not state that product teams struggle to envision products around capabilities that do not yet exist.

astra-6.text:
I think they reinforce each other. Advancing intelligence expands what a product can do, but a more capable model doesn’t automatically become a useful product. You still have to understand what people are trying to accomplish and make that capability reliable and easy to use.

Products also give research a clearer sense of what matters. When people use a model for real tasks, you discover limitations that a benchmark might miss: perhaps it understands the request but needs too much guidance, or it performs well most of the time but fails in a way that makes it difficult to trust.

So I see it as a feedback loop. Research creates new possibilities, and product development helps turn those possibilities into value while revealing the next problems to solve. The important thing is to keep those two efforts closely connected.

r001.rationale: The response describes research and product development as reinforcing each other in a feedback loop, rather than as roughly orthogonal pursuits.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as a feedback loop. Advancing intelligence expands what a product can do, but building a useful product teaches us what intelligence actually needs to deliver. A model might perform well on a benchmark and still struggle to understand someone’s intent or complete a task reliably.

So the challenge is to connect capability with usefulness. You put the technology in people’s hands, learn where it helps and where it falls short, and use those lessons to guide further research. Better models enable better products, and real product use helps us ask better research questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence advancement and product development as a feedback loop, not as roughly orthogonal pursuits.

r002.rationale: The response does not say product teams have difficulty envisioning products based on intelligence capabilities that do not yet exist.
